### 4.22 The notifications: only what is new, and the page's own reads

Added 2026-11-25 (forclaude/notifications-page-plan-1.md, FINAL on the
user's word, its steps 1 and 2; section 11): the wallet's read of the
notifications of every 5 seconds gets only what is new, and the
Notifications page has a new look, with filters over the list, "Show
older" under it, and everything marked read when the page opens. Until
then every such read got the newest 100 notifications whole, the read
ones too: 4.9 KB every 5 seconds for a person with 20 notifications and
24.6 KB for a person with 100 or more, counted from the form of the
answer. The user, 2026-11-25: "I don't think we ever fixed it so that
it won't ask the masterpod for every single notification every time. It
should only be asking for new ones." The masterpod's side is its own
spec's section 34, which holds the rule, the counter and the number,
the changes of the two routes and what is left as it is. The masterpod
gained three things there. A running number on every notification,
`seq`, from a counter of its own in the database, the sequence
`notification_seq`. Three fields more in the body of
/list-notifications, `since`, `before` and `kinds`, with each row's
`seq` in its answer and three numbers of the pod's whole list, `seq`,
`count` and `unread`. And a second form of the body of
/mark-notifications-read, `upTo`. No new route, no table, no env
variable and no npm package.

    POST /list-notifications (session), three fields more in the body, one more in each row and three in the answer
    body: { unreadOnly, limit, since, before, kinds }, all optional; a field that is absent, or null, is not named
          limit: the most rows an answer holds, 1 to 500; 100 when it is not named, as before
          since: only the rows with a seq above it, a whole number from 0 to 9007199254740991; a since of 0 is a
                 since
          before: only the rows with a seq below it, a whole number from 1 to 9007199254740991
          kinds: only rows of these kinds, a list of 1 to 21 of the twenty-one kind names, each once
    answer: 200 { notifications: [ { notificationNumber, kind, referenceId, read, createdAt, seq } ], seq, count,
            unread }
            notifications: the rows that fit, the highest seq first, at most limit of them
            seq: the highest seq among the caller's notifications, 0 when there is none; the number to send as
                 the next since
            count: how many notifications the caller has
            unread: how many of them are unread
            count and unread are of all the caller's rows, whatever the body asks for
            nothing new: {"notifications":[],"seq":812,"count":57,"unread":2}, 52 bytes
    checks: 400 bad request shape for a body that names both since and before; then 400 invalid unreadOnly,
            invalid limit, invalid since, invalid before, invalid kinds
    a masterpod of before: reads unreadOnly and limit alone, and answers { notifications }, with no seq in a row

    POST /mark-notifications-read (session), a second form of the body
    body: { notificationNumbers }, 1 to 500 ids, as before, or { upTo }, a whole number from 0 to
          9007199254740991
    writes, with upTo: every unread notification of the caller whose seq is upTo or lower is marked read
    answer: 200 { marked }, how many rows were marked, as before
    checks: 400 bad request shape for a body that names both forms or neither; 400 invalid upTo
    a masterpod of before: answers a body with upTo with 400 bad request shape

What the wallet sends, four bodies of /list-notifications and one of
/mark-notifications-read:

    the first read after a login or a page load    { "limit": 30 }
    every 5 seconds, on every page                 { "since": 812 }
    a tap on a filter, here Security               { "limit": 30, "kinds": ["passkeyAdded", "transferWaiting",
                                                   "recoveryMoveWaiting", "recoveryCaseOpened",
                                                   "alertSettingsChanged"] }
    a tap on "Show older"                          { "limit": 30, "before": 771 }, with kinds when a filter is on
    the page opens, or a row arrives on it         { "upTo": 812 }, to /mark-notifications-read

Until this step the wallet sent { "unreadOnly": false } every 5 seconds
and the ids of the rows to mark; it sends neither any more. A page is 30
rows (`NOTIFICATIONS_PAGE`, constants.ts).

What the wallet does with it (session.service, the shell's poll and the
Notifications page; 8.1, 8.2, 8.3):

- The list and its three numbers. The wallet keeps the list in memory,
  session.notifications, newest first, as before, and three numbers
  beside it: session.notificationsSeq, session.notificationsCount and
  session.unread, the `seq`, `count` and `unread` of the answer that
  was last put into the list. The list is null until the first answer.
- The first read. While the list has no `seq`, the shell's read asks
  for { "limit": 30 }: that is the first read after a login or a page
  load. Its answer is the list.
- The read on the timer (`readNotifications()` in app.ts). Every later
  read sends the list's `seq` as `since`. The rows that come back go on
  top of the list, and the answer's three numbers are the list's. When
  no row came, the list is not set anew, so nothing that draws from it
  is worked out again. One thing more: when such an answer says that
  nothing is unread, every row in memory is read, whatever it said when
  the row came, since the answer of a mark can be lost on its way.
- The compare. Before the rows are put in, the wallet compares. When
  the answer's `count` is not the count it had plus the rows that came,
  it missed a row: more rows were new than one answer holds, or a
  notification was committed after a later-numbered one (the
  masterpod's spec, 34.3). When the answer's `seq` is below the `since`
  that was sent, the masterpod's database was put back from a backup.
  In both cases the wallet reads the first page again, once, and that
  answer takes the list's place. When that read fails, the list and its
  numbers stay as they were, and the next read on the timer finds the
  same thing again.
- Answers in another order. An answer of the shell's read is put in
  only while the list's `seq` is still the one the read was asked with.
  It is also dropped when the answer of a mark came between the asking
  and the answer: such an answer can carry the rows and the unread
  number of before the mark. The next read brings what a dropped answer
  held.
- The number in the menu and on Home is session.unread: all of the
  pod's unread notifications, as the masterpod counts them, and not
  only the rows in memory.
- The page's own reads. The Notifications page (8.2) asks the masterpod
  for rows in three cases only: the first page, when the page is opened
  in the first seconds after a login, before the shell's poll has read
  it; a filter's first page; and "Show older". The last two change
  neither the list's `seq` nor its count: they bring rows for the page.
- A filter's list. A tap on a filter shows at once the rows of that
  group which the list in memory holds, and the page reads the filter's
  first page, { "limit": 30, "kinds": [...] }. Which kinds make a group
  is the wallet's list (8.2); the masterpod knows no groups. The rows
  of the answer take the place of the rows shown, and with them stand,
  on top, the rows of the group that the list in memory holds with a
  `seq` above the highest `seq` of the filter's own rows: those are the
  rows that the shell's read has brought since. When the filter's own
  rows are none, every row of the group that the list in memory holds
  is shown. The plan's section 7 words this otherwise: "with the rows
  of that group that the timer brings put on top". Taken to the letter
  that shows a row twice: a notification that was written after the
  shell's last read is above the `since` of its next one, can already
  be on the filter's first page, and comes again with that next read.
  Leaving out the rows whose id the filter's rows hold is not enough
  either: when more rows of a group came at once than a page holds, the
  shell's read brings rows that belong below the filter's first page,
  and they would stand on top. The masterpod's build found both in its
  trial (its spec, 34.5 and 34.8), and this step's trial showed both in
  the built page (section 11). The filter's rows belong to the page and
  are gone when another filter is picked or the page is left.
- "Show older". Under All it stands while the list in memory holds
  fewer rows than `count`, under a filter while the last read for that
  filter came back full, with 30 rows. A tap reads { "limit": 30,
  "before": N }, with the group's `kinds` under a filter, N being the
  lowest `seq` the page shows. Under All the rows go to the end of the
  list in memory, under a filter to the end of the filter's rows. The
  answer is put in only while the row it was asked below is still the
  lowest one. Under All its rows are put in as read: an older row that
  was still unread was marked with the rest when the page opened, or is
  marked now, so it has no dot.
- The first page again, with a filter on. When the shell reads the
  first page again because it missed a row, the page with a filter on
  reads that filter's first page again too, and the rows that came with
  "Show older" fold back to the first 30
  (session.notificationPages counts the first pages that were put in).
- Marking. Opening the page marks everything read: one request,
  /mark-notifications-read with { "upTo": the list's seq }. The page
  sends it when it opens with something unread, and when a row arrives
  while it is open: each time the list in memory or the unread number
  changes while something is unread. It sends nothing while the unread
  number is 0, while the list has no `seq`, and while a mark is on its
  way. After the answer every row of the list up to that number is
  read, and the unread number is the rows above it that are still
  unread: none, unless a row arrived while the mark was on its way,
  which the next mark then covers at once. A notification that was
  written after the wallet's last read has a higher `seq`, so it is not
  marked; it comes with the next read, as a new row. A mark that fails
  changes nothing: the number stays, and the next change of the list
  sends it again, which is a row that arrives or the page opened again.
  A read on the timer with nothing new does not send it again.
- The dots. The rows that were unread when the page opened and the rows
  that arrived while it was open keep a dot and a bold sentence for as
  long as the page is open: their ids are kept on the page and are gone
  with it. A row that comes with "Show older" was marked with the rest
  when the page opened, so it comes read and has no dot. A row of a
  filter's first page that is above the list's `seq` was written after
  the shell's last read, so it arrived while the page is open: it has
  its dot at once, before the shell's read brings it.
- The words that depend on the clock. The time under a sentence is
  worded by the clock ("Just now", "5 min ago", "3 h ago",
  "Yesterday"). session.minute is the clock's minute as a signal. Every
  read of the shell looks at the clock, and the page's rows read the
  signal, so the words are drawn again each minute and at midnight with
  nothing else set anew. chat.service's `today` (4.17) is no use here:
  it moves only once setup is complete, and the rows of the vouching
  come before that.
- A masterpod of before. An answer without `seq`, `count` and `unread`
  is taken as the first page: its rows are the list, the list has no
  `seq`, its count is the rows that came and its unread number the
  unread rows among them, so the next read asks for the first page
  again. That is also a masterpod server that still runs the old code
  during the masterpod's own deploy. Nothing more is built for it, by
  the plan: against such a server no mark is sent, "Show older" does
  not stand, and a filter shows the newest 30 rows of every kind, since
  the old code does not read `kinds`. So this step is deployed only
  once the masterpod's step runs on every masterpod server.
- A read that is refused or not answered changes nothing, and the next
  one asks again. A read of the page that fails shows the red line,
  "/list-notifications: HTTP 503: ...", unless nobody waits for it any
  more: the page's own first read when the shell's has brought the list
  meanwhile, and an older page when another filter was tapped
  meanwhile.

Decided while building, where the plan left a point of the code open,
each the smallest way seen:

1. Where the code is. No new file. The list, its numbers and the three
   ways they change (`putNotifications`, `putNewNotifications`,
   `putNotificationsRead`) are in session.service, the shell's read is
   in app.ts beside the poll, and the page's own reads and the mark are
   in the page. One new constant, `NOTIFICATIONS_PAGE`, stands in
   constants.ts with the wallet's other page sizes; the plan does not
   name that file.
2. The compare comes before the rows are put on top. The plan's 3.3
   words it the other way round. The result is the same whenever the
   read of the first page succeeds. When it fails, the list is as it
   was, and the rows of the next answer are not put in a second time.
3. After a mark's answer the unread number is the unread rows above
   `upTo` that the list holds, where the plan says 0. It is 0 unless a
   row arrived while the mark was on its way.
4. When the page marks. The plan names two moments, the page's opening
   and a row that arrives. The page marks whenever the list in memory
   or the unread number changes while something is unread, which is
   those two moments. After a mark that failed, an older page under All
   sends it again too.
5. A filter's list is worked out from two things each time, the list
   in memory and the page's own rows for the filter, by the rule
   above. The page keeps no record of which rows the shell's read
   brought.
6. "New" is the block of rows with a dot at the top of what is shown,
   and "Earlier" the rest, as the stand-in page of the plan's pictures
   has it. A row never moves. A row with a dot below a row without one
   keeps its place and its dot; with marking up to a number that needs
   the gap of the masterpod's 34.7.
7. A tap on the filter that is on takes it off, and All is on. A tap on
   All while it is on leaves it on: Material's list of chips would
   take the mark off and show no filter as on.
8. A page with no row says "No notifications yet." or "No notifications
   of this kind." only once it knows that there is none: under All
   when the wallet has its list, under a filter when the masterpod has
   answered for it. The red line of a read that failed goes when a
   first page is put into the list.
9. The mark and the page's reads are quiet: they are not in the Log
   (8.2, Log), as the shell's reads are not.
10. `listNotifications` takes the body as one object, and
    `markNotificationsRead` the number. `NotificationsAnswer` and the
    row's `seq` are in session.service beside `NotificationItem`; the
    three numbers and the row's `seq` are optional in the types, since
    a masterpod of before sends none.
11. Four things came from a second reader's read of the code against
    the plan (section 11), each a few lines and each built: a row of a
    filter's first page that the shell's read has not brought yet has
    its dot at once; an older page's rows under All are put in as read,
    where the build had first dropped an older page that crossed a
    mark; an answer that says nothing is unread makes every row in
    memory read; and a refusal that nobody waits for sets no red line.
    A fifth was left as it is: when a row arrives while a mark is on
    its way and that mark then fails, the row is not marked until the
    next change of the list.

What a person sees is in 8.2, Notifications. What travels down to the
phone, counted at the trial's front as bytes of an answer's body
(section 11): 54 bytes every 5 seconds while nothing is new, where the
newest 100 came whole; about 310 bytes once for a new notification; and
7.7 KB for the first page of 30 rows after a login, where it was up to
24.6 KB. Opening the page brings no rows. What goes up is as before:
three signed requests every 5 seconds once setup is complete and two
before that, about 9.6 KB each (section 10); a mark is one request
where a press of the old button was two.

One gap is known and left as it is, by the masterpod's spec (its 34.7):
two notifications for one pod are written at the same instant and
committed in the other order than their numbers, the wallet's read
falls between the two commits, and the page marks before the wallet's
next read. The row with the lower number is then marked before the
wallet was sent it: it comes with the first page, in its place and
already read, with no dot, and was never counted in the number.

The proxy forwards both routes as any masterpod path (section 2);
nothing in server/ and nothing under deploy/ changed, and no request
was added, so the doormen count the same calls as before. The wallet's
side is the shell's poll (8.1; 8.2, Notifications), the Notifications
page and Home's number (8.2), session.service (8.3) and the words
(8.8).

## 5. Validator changes (anossoftware)

### 5.1 A nonces table and two variables

db/schema.sql gets the keyholder's nonces table as it is (nonce BYTEA PK
16 to 32 bytes, expires_at, the index). `npm run db:setup` adds it to
anos1 to anos5 without a reset. env.js gets two optional variables:
MASTERPOD_URL (default http://localhost:3100) and
TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_SECONDS (default 120), read through an optional helper
like the masterpod's. The five env files need no edit.

### 5.2 The binding check on /create-account

verifyCreateAccount gets a fifth check after uniqueness: POST
MASTERPOD_URL/get-anos-account { accountId } (src/masterpod/
masterpod.client.js, 5-second timeout, shaped like the keyholder's
client). It passes only on a 200 whose anopodId decodes to 32 bytes and
whose vouched is true. Anything else, a 404, a timeout, a 5xx, a bad
body, vouched false, refuses the submission with 400 { error: "bad
request" } and writes no log line: the request is dropped like garbage,
as decided. Only the receiving validator asks; the validator-to-validator
approval path trusts it, as it does for everything else.

### 5.3 The account level

A fourth kind of caller: an account signing with pair one, for reads.
src/auth/ gets signed-request.js (parseSignedRequest and verifyBoth),
common-checks.js and nonces.queries.js, copied from keyholdersoftware
with their comments pointed at this server, and require-account.js:

1. Shape: { payload: { accountId, path, timestamp, nonce, body },
   signatures: { ecdsa, mldsa } }, every field a string, body an object.
   400 bad request shape.
2. payload.path equals the route. 401 path mismatch.
3. The timestamp within TIMESTAMP_WINDOW_SECONDS of now, either way. 401
   timestamp outside window.
4. accountId decodes to 32 bytes (400 invalid accountId); an accounts row
   (401 unknown account); both signatures over the canonical payload
   against public_key1 and public_key_pq1 (401 bad signature).
5. The nonce, 16 to 32 bytes (400 invalid nonce), new in nonces (401
   replay), kept twice the window.
6. req.account = the id, req.body = payload.body.

### 5.4 The two reads

src/reads/ (router, handlers, service, queries), wired in app.js. All
five answer the signer's own account only; nothing about anyone else.
Since 2026-11-08 two public reads sit beside them, /list-fund-proposals
and /get-fund-proposal, the block at the end of this section.
The third, /list-escrows, was added 2026-11-05 for the escrow trades
(anossoftware spec section 16); the fourth, /get-assisted-transfer, on
2026-11-06 for the assisted transfer (anossoftware spec section 17); the
fifth, /get-locked-transfer, and the date range on /list-transactions on
2026-11-06 for the balances and the history (anossoftware spec section
18).

    POST /get-account (account)
    body { }
    answer: 200 { accountId, type, balance: millionths as a decimal string, latestTransactionId: hex | null,
      createdAt: ISO 8601, stakes: { daoVote, moderator, attestor, guardian, validator, masterPod },
      guardianVotes: number }. latestTransactionId is the transaction_id of the garlic_chain link with the
      highest position whose account_id is the signer: what the next transfer names as previousTransactionId.
    stakes and guardianVotes (2026-11-08, anossoftware spec 25.1): the account's stake per purpose, millionths
      as decimal strings, "0" each when the account has no stakes row, and floor(guardian / GUARDIAN_VOTE_ANOS)
      as a number, the account's guardian votes. A validator without the fund proposal reads sends neither;
      the wallet's AccountAnswer has both optional. The Guardians pages and Home's fund proposal line read
      guardianVotes. Since 2026-11-10 (section 11, forclaude/wallet-balance-card-plan-1.md) the balances
      service (8.3) reads stakes, for the balance card (8.2, Wallet): it keeps each account's purposes above
      zero and adds them up as Staked, which the card counts into Total, since a stake is a transfer to the
      fund and has left the balance. An answer without stakes counts as nothing staked.

    POST /list-transactions (account)
    body { beforePosition?: integer, limit?: integer (default 50, at most 200), from?: ISO 8601, to?: ISO 8601 }
    answer: 200 { transactions: [ { transactionId, position, type, accountId, accountIdTo, amount: string,
      createdAt } ], pending: [ { transactionId, type, accountId, accountIdTo, amount: string, createdAt,
      approved } ] }
    transactions: garlic_chain links where account_id or account_id_to is the signer, position descending,
      below beforePosition when given, with created_at at or after from and before to when given, limit rows;
      createdAt the row's created_at. pending: the signer's pending row (there is at most one), fields read
      from og_transaction.payload (transactionType, accountIdTo, amount or "0", createdAt). The other holding
      tables (locked, assisted, escrow, fund proposals) are not listed here; a guarded transfer shows up when
      it lands (section 10), the open escrows have /list-escrows and the locked transfer /get-locked-transfer.
    from and to (2026-11-06, anossoftware spec 18.3): either alone works; to is the first moment after the
      range, so the wallet sends the start of the day after the last day picked; beforePosition and limit work
      as before, within the range; pending is not cut. A value Date.parse does not accept is 400 invalid from
      or 400 invalid to.

    POST /list-escrows (account)
    body { }
    answer: 200 { escrows: [ { transactionId, accountId, accountIdTo, amount: string, createdAt,
      stage: waiting | held | releasing | cancelling | disputed, disputedBy: hex | null,
      verdicts: [ { verdict: success | cancel, approved } ] } ] }
    escrows: the escrow_transfers rows where account_id (the seller) or account_id_to (the buyer) is the
      signer, newest first, at most 200: the open trades only, nothing from logs (which may be purged) or
      archives. A released escrow is on the chain under the same id, so /list-transactions shows it to
      both sides for good; a cancelled one leaves no trace the wallet reads. stage is named by the
      validator from the row's columns (anossoftware spec 16.2): waiting until every validator accepted
      the trade (no follow-up is accepted on it yet); held when nothing is signed on it; releasing with
      the seller's success on it; cancelling with the buyer's cancel on it; disputed with a dispute on it,
      which only verdicts move. disputedBy is the signer of the dispute. verdicts carry what each verdict
      says and whether every validator accepted it, never the attestor's id.

    POST /get-assisted-transfer (account)
    body { }
    answer: 200 { transfer: { transactionId, type, accountId, accountIdTo, amount: string, createdAt,
      stage: waiting | attesting | locked | writing | cancelling, attestations: 0 | 1 | 2,
      unlocksAt: ISO 8601 | null } | null }
    transfer: the assisted_transfers row whose account_id is the signer, or null when there is none. There is
      at most one: account_id is unique there, and the validator holds one transaction per account. The
      sender's only: the receiver can do nothing with the transfer and sees it in the history when it lands.
      The held transfer only, nothing from logs or archives: a written transfer is on the chain under the
      same id, so /list-transactions shows it for good; a cancelled one leaves no trace the wallet reads.
      stage is named by the validator from the row's columns (anossoftware spec 17.2): waiting until every
      validator accepted the transfer (no follow-up is accepted on it yet); cancelling with the sender's
      cancel on it; writing with both attestations approved, until the next round writes it (the sender may
      still cancel); attesting otherwise, accepted and waiting for two approved attestations. attestations
      counts the attestation slots holding one; the two reach the validator together, posted by the
      deciding attestor's app, so it is nearly always 0 or 2. Since 2026-11-08 (anossoftware spec 22) the
      row may be a breakGlassTransfer, the recovery finish's move out of a lost account (12.3): unlocksAt is
      then the moment a move out of a guarded or vault account may be written (null for every other row),
      and a fifth stage, locked, is both attestations approved with that moment ahead; the wallet reads it
      "Locked until <date>" (assistedStages.locked).
    type (answered by the validator since 2026-11-08, read by the wallet since 2026-11-10,
      forclaude/recovery-finish-order-plan-1.md): the row's transactionType, assistedAnosTransfer or
      breakGlassTransfer. Since 2026-11-10 this read is also made with the break-glass pair, by the recovery's
      finish (12.3, Move your money): the envelope is signed by a lost account's break-glass pair, which the
      account level accepts as it does on /get-account (anossoftware spec 22). A breakGlassTransfer in the
      answer is a move the validators already hold for that account, and its transactionId and accountIdTo
      are what the finish files with the masterpod. Every other read of it is signed by pair one.

    POST /get-locked-transfer (account)
    body { }
    answer: 200 { transfer: { transactionId, accountId, accountIdTo, amount: string, createdAt,
      unlocksAt: ISO 8601, stage: waiting | locked | due | cancelling } | null }
    transfer: the locked_transactions row whose account_id is the signer, a guarded or vault transfer waiting
      out its time lock, or null when there is none (2026-11-06, anossoftware spec section 18). There is at
      most one: account_id is unique there, and the validator holds one transaction per account. The sender's
      only: the receiver sees it in the history when it lands. The held transfer only, nothing from logs or
      archives: a written transfer is on the chain under the same id, and the row is deleted when written.
      Since 2026-11-11 the sender can cancel a locked transfer until it is written, with the follow-up
      lockedTransferCancel at POST /locked-transfer-cancel (anossoftware spec section 28; 8.2, Account). A
      cancelled transfer's row moves to the validator's logs, and this read then answers null: a cancelled
      transfer leaves no trace the wallet reads. Until that day nothing could be done with a locked
      transfer, since no follow-up existed for it. unlocksAt is the row's
      future_date, the moment the transfer may be written. stage is named by the validator from the row by the
      database's clock, the one the ready list reads (anossoftware spec 18.2): waiting until every validator
      accepted the transfer; cancelling (2026-11-11) with the sender's cancel on it, which the validator
      decides right after waiting, until every validator accepted the cancel and the row is gone; locked
      while the unlock moment is ahead; due once it has passed, until the next
      leader round writes it (a round starts with the next transaction of any kind).

Refusals are 400 or 401 + { error }, logged "failed: <reason>" like
every other route. The 1 MB JSON limit stays.

The public reads (2026-11-08; anossoftware spec 25, the plan
forclaude/wallet-guardians-plan-1.md): no envelope, no signature, the body
a plain JSON object (400 bad request shape otherwise), built like
/list-dao-stakes (anossoftware 23); the doorman passes them at 4 KB with
the object check (doormansoftware spec 7), the fields are the validator's.
Everything they answer is the fund's business: a written proposal's
payouts are on the public chain, and the votes are the guardians' public
act on the fund's money. A validator or a doorman without them answers
404, which the wallet shows in red under the tab of the Guardians page
while everything else works, so the validators and their doormen deploy
first.

    POST /list-fund-proposals (public)
    body { status: 'open' | 'decided', limit?: integer (default 20, at most 200), offset?: integer, from?: ISO 8601, to?: ISO 8601 }
    answer: 200 { settings, proposals: [ item ] }
    settings: { anosPerVote, minimumStake, percent, minutes }, the validator's GUARDIAN_VOTE_ANOS and
      STAKE_MIN_GUARDIAN_ANOS as millionths (decimal strings) and GUARDIAN_VOTE_PERCENT and GUARDIAN_VOTE_MINUTES
      as numbers, with every answer, so the wallet's notice, its rule and its become-a-guardian sentence carry
      the validator's own numbers.
    item: { transactionId, guardianId (the proposer's account), createdAt, voteClosesAt, status, approved,
      payoutCount, total: millionths as a decimal string, forWeight (the proposer's weight plus the approved
      votes for), againstWeight (the approved votes against), passing, decidedAt: ISO 8601 | null,
      votes: [ { guardianId, vote: for | against, weight, approved, votedAt } ] } (anossoftware 25.1).
    status (anossoftware 25.2): waiting until every validator accepted the proposal (no vote is accepted on it
      yet); open while voteClosesAt is ahead; closing once it has passed and the next ready list has not tallied
      it yet; written for an archived proposal that passed and whose payouts the round wrote; failed for one that
      did not. A word the wallet does not know is shown as it is, with no button.
    open lists the fund_proposals rows, one at most (limit, offset, from and to are not read); decided lists the
      archives rows of fund proposals, newest first by the decision, after offset rows, with the decision at or
      after from and before to when given (to is the first moment after the range, as /list-transactions takes
      them). 400 invalid status / invalid limit / invalid offset / invalid from / invalid to.

    POST /get-fund-proposal (public)
    body { transactionId: hex }
    answer: 200 { settings, proposal }, the item plus proposerWeight (the proposer's votes when the proposal was
      stored) and payouts: [ { index, accountIdTo, amount, reason, stakeFor: purpose | null } ] in index order,
      the fields as the proposer sent them; the open row first, then the archives. 400 invalid transactionId
      for anything but 64 hex characters; 404 unknown proposal.

## 6. The keyholders

Since 2026-11-08 the wallet also asks every keyholder `/get-owner` (level
none, keyholder spec section 15) who owns a lookup id, all at once with
the deposit's 15 second limit, found when any answers: the locked-out
stepper's step 1 (12.3), `SharesService.findOwner`. Before that, nothing
here changed keyholdersoftware. What the wallet sends them in a deposit is
what the keyholder test app sends, with the stand-ins replaced:

- publicLedgerId: the real PLID, 32 bytes (docs/public-ledger-id.md).
- lookupId: the real rule, section 6 there.
- shareType: backupcode at setup, securitybucket1 and securitybucket2 at
  each bucket add, and breakglasskey at each anos account creation, the
  type nothing sent before.
- keyId: 32 random bytes per secret, the same on every keyholder, and
  (new) the same value the masterpod gets with the bucket add.

The deposit rule, everywhere a secret is made (as changed 2026-11-07 by
forclaude/wallet-deposit-floor-plan-1.md; before it every keyholder had
to answer 201, one at a time, in order)
1. The secret is split into as many shares as /api/config says
   keyholders, threshold shareThreshold, with shamir-secret-sharing as
   today. Shares and threshold are separate numbers: 27 keyholders get
   exactly 27 shares, nothing is computed and thrown away.
2. Share n goes to keyholder n through /api/keyholder/n/receive-share,
   the receiving key fetched through /api/keyholder/n/get-keyholder-public-key
   once per session, every keyholder at once, each call with a time limit
   of 15 seconds (KEYHOLDER_DEPOSIT_TIMEOUT_MS in constants.ts): a
   keyholder that has not answered by then counts as one that did not
   store the share, so a stopped VM holds nobody for the proxy's two
   minutes.
3. The deposit goes through when at least the floor stored it:
   depositFloorPercent of the keyholders, rounded up, never below
   shareThreshold (22 of 27 at 80 percent; every keyholder when the proxy
   sends no percent). The masterpod step that follows (complete-setup,
   the bucket add, create-anos-account) then runs; the keyholders that
   failed show only in the activity log. Below the floor the step stops:
   the screen says how many stored, how many were needed and the first
   failure ("Only 20 of 27 keyholders stored the share, 22 are needed.
   Keyholder 12: HTTP 0: no answer in 15 s"), and Retry starts the step
   again with a fresh secret and a fresh keyId. The shares already stored
   are orphans under a keyId nothing names; reads list newest first, so
   they never get in the way.
4. So "stored on the masterpod" means "enough keyholders have it". A
   keyholder that was down misses that share for good; the secret still
   rebuilds from any shareThreshold of the others, and the reads already
   tolerate a missing share (a pull needs the threshold, not everyone).
   A catch-up that hands a keyholder the shares it missed is not built
   (the plan's decision 1). No temporary table, no state column.

## 7. Client crypto, new or changed

Everything the three test apps compute stays as the records say
(masterpod rules/client_crypto.md, keyholder rules/client_crypto.md, anos
flows/how_a_wallet_builds_a_transaction.md). New or changed:

    PLID, lookupId      docs/public-ledger-id.md; scrypt from @noble/hashes/scrypt, SHA-256 from @noble/hashes
    identityBlob        AES-256-GCM under the encryption key of PLID (32) || lookupId (32): iv || ciphertext || tag, 92 bytes
    break-glass seed    32 random bytes per anos account. breakGlassKey: P-256 scalar = HKDF(seed, "anos/break-glass-p256/v1", 48)
                        as an integer mod (n - 1), plus 1, the backup code's rule; breakGlassPostQuantumKey: ML-DSA-87
                        keygen(HKDF(seed, "anos/break-glass-mldsa/v1", 32)). HKDF-SHA-256, empty salt. The seed is
                        split and deposited as breakglasskey, then wiped; it is never sent to the masterpod. At a
                        recovery's finish the recovered seed signs the account's break-glass move (step 5 of
                        forclaude/break-glass-plan-1.md) and is wiped again; nothing of it is stored on the
                        masterpod (2026-11-08; from 2026-10-26 to then the finish stored it as breakGlassBlob).
    keyBlob             AES-256-GCM under the key blob key of key1 scalar (32) || postQuantumKey1 seed (32) ||
                        key2 scalar (32) || postQuantumKey2 seed (32), 156 bytes. The key blob key (2026-11-08,
                        forclaude/break-glass-plan-1.md) = HKDF(PRF output, "masterpod/kek-keys/v1", 32): from the
                        passkey's PRF output alone, a sibling of KEK_prf, derived at every unlock and create and
                        kept in RAM with the PRF output (session.service); not the encryption key, which the backup
                        code also opens, so a backup-code recovery returns the pod and not the signing keys, and
                        losing every passkey of the anoPod loses the key blobs for good (the wallet shows such an
                        account as lost, 8.2).
                        ML-DSA-87 keys come back from their seeds (the test wallet's generateMlDsaKey(seed)), P-256
                        public keys from the scalars. Opened only to sign, then dropped; the ciphertext stays in
                        RAM for the session. Before 2026-11-08 the blob was under the encryption key.
                        Since 2026-11-20 (4.11) this is the blob with both pairs, and it is kept at the masterpod: a
                        new account sends it once, and the wallet is handed it, as keyBlob in the answer of
                        /list-anos-accounts, only until the account has a first key blob (the next row). From
                        then on what the wallet holds and opens to sign is the first key blob.
    firstKeyBlob (2026-11-20)
                        AES-256-GCM under the key blob key of key1 scalar (32) || postQuantumKey1 seed (32), 92
                        bytes: pair one alone (wrapFirstKeyBlob, crypto.service). Pair two is not in it. Made with
                        a new account, beside the keyBlob, and, for an account that has none yet, at the person's
                        next login (unlock.ts; 4.11), where it is opened again and its two public keys are compared
                        with key1 and postQuantumKey1 in the account's creation before it is sent. The masterpod
                        stores it once (first_key_blob) and from then on answers it as keyBlob, with firstKeyOnly
                        true. pairOneFromKeyBlob (crypto.service) opens both kinds of blob: 64 bytes inside, or 128,
                        of which the first 64 are pair one; anything else throws "keyBlob must open to 64 or 128
                        bytes".
    the wallet pair     asked for every new account from /api/sign/<n>/public-keys (2026-11-13, section 11; fetched
                        once per session until then): a signing server answers one of its pairs, picked at random,
                        and the account names that pair for life; a creation payload carries them as
                        walletKey and walletPostQuantumKey; the browser makes the other six signatures and
                        /api/sign/<n> adds the two. Every transfer, fund proposal and follow-up is signed by pair one
                        in the browser and by the wallet pair through /api/sign/<n>, the signer account's creation
                        payload sent along (section 3), then posted to the validator. Since 2026-11-20 the
                        passkey's answer for the thing goes along as well (the two rows after this one; section 3).
    the fingerprint of a thing to sign (2026-11-20)
                        the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes of its payload, the same bytes pair one signs and a
                        signing server signs, as 64 lowercase hex characters (fingerprint, crypto.service).
    the challenge of a signing passkey (2026-11-20)
                        the SHA-256 of the fixed label anos/signing-passkey/v1: followed by the fingerprints, joined
                        by commas (signingChallenge, crypto.service; the label is SIGNING_PASSKEY_LABEL there and
                        in the signing server's src/sign.js, and a new rule for the challenge gets a new label).
                        For one transfer that is one fingerprint. For "Sign all attestations" it is one per move.
                        One answer covers at most 100 fingerprints. The passkey that opened the session answers it
                        (askSigningPasskey, 8.9). The signing server works the challenge out again from the list
                        that came with the request, after it has found the fingerprint of its own payload in that
                        list. So an answer is good for exactly the things the person's tap built, and a payload
                        changed afterwards has another fingerprint.
    the account envelope for reads
                        { payload: { accountId, path, timestamp, nonce, body }, signatures: { ecdsa, mldsa } }:
                        the pod envelope with accountId as the signer field, signed by pair one (P-256 r||s over
                        the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes, ML-DSA-87 over the bytes), nonce 16 random bytes.
    the bucket keyId    sent with the add as well as in the deposits.
    the backup code     never shown (2026-11-10, section 11): made at Setup, wrapped as blob2 and deposited with the
                        keyholders as backupcode, all without the person seeing it or writing it down; it is the
                        secret the long recovery rebuilds from the bankers' shares. Until 2026-11-10 it was shown
                        once as base32 in groups of four, with a Complete button.
    the wallet pair of the test wallet
                        wallet-keys.ts is not carried over.
    noteBlob (2026-11-07)
                        AES-256-GCM under the encryption key of the UTF-8 JSON { v: 1, kind, money, currency, memo, tag }:
                        a few hundred bytes; wrapJson / unwrapJson (crypto.service)
    settingsBlob (2026-11-07)
                        the same of { v: 1, protect }
    wrappedKeyBlobKey (2026-11-18)
                        AES-256-GCM of the key blob key under HKDF(the added passkey's PRF output,
                        "masterpod/kek-keys-wrap/v1", 32), 60 bytes; the main passkey has none and makes the key blob
                        key from its PRF output as before. Made when a passkey is added, from the PRF output of one
                        sign-in with the new passkey (8.2, Passkeys); kept by the masterpod on that passkey's
                        added_passkeys row and answered by /unlock (4.8); opened at every unlock with that passkey
                        (deriveKekKeysWrap, crypto.service), and a copy that does not open ends the unlock. The
                        added passkey's blob1 is made as the first one is: the encryption key under KEK_prf of that
                        passkey's own PRF output.
    passkeyNames (2026-11-18)
                        a field of the settings object, so inside settingsBlob, which is now the same of
                        { v: 1, protect, passkeyNames }: a map from an added passkey's passkey id (hex) to the name
                        the person gave it, 1 to 40 characters. The main passkey has no entry. The masterpod stores
                        no name and cannot read one.

## 8. The web app (src/)

Angular 22, standalone components, signals, the router, Angular Material
22 with a prebuilt theme and no custom styling, web first: a toolbar and
a side navigation on a desktop, the navigation collapsing behind a menu
button on a phone. Everything secret lives in RAM and dies with the tab,
as in the test apps; a new tab unlocks again. (Since 2026-11-24 one
thing of a pod's outlives the tab: the chat with Joy that is under way,
kept in the browser's own database as a blob under the anoPod
encryption key, which only the passkey brings back; 4.18, section 11.)
(Since 2026-11-25 a second thing does: a copy of the thread of each
chat room the person has opened, kept the same way, one blob for each
room, in a database of the rooms' own; 8.2, Chat, 8.3 and section 11.)
(Since 2026-11-25 also a third: the pictures that Joy had made for the
chat that is under way, each a blob of its own under the same key, in
Joy's database beside the chat; 4.21, section 11.)

### 8.1 Shell, routes, guards

    /                        landing: Log in, Create account, Recover account
    /create                  the create stepper
    /recover                 "Coming soon: under construction during Test Net"
    /vouching                find seeds, send requests, wait
    /identity                the public ledger id: why, the form, the review
    /setup                   keys, the backup code, the deposits, complete-setup
    /account                 your account: a plain list of rows, Account recovery, Passkeys, Public ledger id, Sound and Security alerts
    /account/recovery        the Account recovery page: Recovery selfie and Recovery details, with what is on file
    /account/recovery/selfie    the account recovery walkthrough, opened at the selfie
    /account/recovery/details   the walkthrough opened at the ID
    /account/protect         the Protect your passkey page: the setup pane again, Save records the answer
    /account/passkeys        the Passkeys page: the anoPod's passkeys, and the three steps that add one
    /account/ledger-id       the Public ledger id page: the birth record typed again, and whether it gives the same id
    /account/alerts          the Security alerts page: the emails and the phones that are told when a transfer starts to wait, with Take off and Keep
    /security/bucket-one     forwards to /account/recovery/selfie
    /security/bucket-two     forwards to /account/recovery/details
    /home                    home: the greeting, the balance card, things to do, the tiles
    /wallet                  the anos accounts and Create anos account
    /wallet/:accountId       one account: balance, send, pending, escrow trades, the held or locked transfer
    /wallet/:accountId/escrow/:transactionId   one escrow trade: the details, the buttons for your side, the closed view
    /wallet/:accountId/assisted/:transactionId   one assisted transfer: the details, the stage, the case, Cancel transfer, the closed view
    /wallet/:accountId/history   the transaction history: the rows in plain words by day, a date range, Show more
    /wallet/notes            the noted transactions: every account's notes, a date range, the kind chips, the totals, Download as CSV
    /chat                    the list of chats; on a desktop the pane beside it shows the child route
    /chat/requests           invites to me and join requests on my rooms
    /chat/new                start a chat: Message someone, Find public rooms, New public room
    /chat/:chatRoomId        one conversation
    /joy                     Joy, the wallet's AI: the one chat with her, Memory, New chat (2026-11-24, 4.18)
    /joy/memory              Joy's memory of the member: the file's text, Save, Delete all (2026-11-24, 4.18)
    /marketplace             browse: the filter chips, the Your listings row, the cards

    /marketplace/mine        your listings, open first, with who connected and Close

    /dao                     DAO: the notice, three tabs (Open votes, Pending, Decided), the cards, New proposal

    /dao/guardians           Guardians: the notice, your guardian accounts, two tabs (Open vote, Decided), the cards, New proposal
    /dao/guardians/new       a new fund proposal: the account that proposes, the payouts, Post
    /dao/guardians/:transactionId   one fund proposal: the status, the payouts, the numbers, Voting as and your vote with a confirm in place, the votes

In app.routes.ts the three Guardians routes (2026-11-08, section 11; the
plan is forclaude/wallet-guardians-plan-1.md) sit between dao/new and
dao/:proposalId: the router takes the first route that matches, and
dao/:proposalId would otherwise swallow dao/guardians. The Guardians have
no entry of their own in the side panel or the Home tiles: the DAO page
carries a card to them (8.2).

The route of the person's recovery case, cases/recovery/:caseId
(2026-11-12, section 11; the plan is
forclaude/wallet-case-chats-plan-1.md), sits in front of cases/:caseId
in app.routes.ts, the more specific path first. The Cases routes are not
in the list above: they are in 13.2, and this one is there with them.

A guard sends anyone without a session to /. Which pages the navigation
shows follows the status: vouching until vouched; identity and setup
until setup is complete; home first, then wallet, chat, Joy
(2026-11-24, section 11; 4.18), marketplace, DAO
(2026-11-08) and account once it is (2026-11-06, section 11); seed when
isSeed. The Chat entry carries the number of unread rooms (8.2, Chat;
2026-11-05, section 11) and the Notifications entry the number of unread
notifications (2026-11-06); the side panel and the Home tiles draw one
list, navigation.service (8.3). The toolbar's brand is a link to /home
once setup is complete. Since 2026-11-24 (section 11) the brand is one
short word in bold letters of 18 px: "anoPod", and in the staff's
editions "Moderator" (12.1) and "Attestor" (13.1). It read "anoPod
wallet", "Moderator wallet" and "Attestor wallet" before, in letters of
22 px. The username beside it ends in "…" when the top bar has no room
for all of it.

Two more entries carry a number since 2026-11-12 (section 11; the plan
is forclaude/wallet-case-chats-plan-1.md, its decisions 15 and 25): the
Moderation entry of the moderator edition (12.3) and the Attesting entry
of the attestor edition (13.3). The number is how many things on that
page this device has not seen yet, as the Chat entry counts its unread
rooms. A thing on the Attesting page is a row of its three lists: an
assisted transfer the validators hold, a disputed escrow the validators
hold, a recovery case that is open or in review. A thing on the
Moderation page is a recovery case that is open or in review. The wallet
reads those lists every 15 seconds, in that edition only, and the number
clears when the page is opened (work-badge.service, 8.3). It shows at
the right of the entry in the side panel and on the entry's Home tile,
since both draw the one list.

The sound (2026-11-19, section 11; the plan is
forclaude/wallet-chat-and-passkey-plan-1.md, its step 5). The wallet has
one sound: two short notes, the second higher, made by the browser's own
sound engine with no sound file (sound.service, 8.3). The shell rings it
from its 5-second poll (8.2, Notifications), once setup is complete,
when an answer of /list-chat-rooms holds something new since the answer
before. New is a newest message by someone else in a room that was in
the answer before, or an invite to this pod or a join request on one of
its rooms that was not in it. A message in the conversation that is the
page on the screen rings nothing: that is the address /chat/<that room>
while the page is visible (the browser's document.visibilityState is
"visible"), so the same conversation in a hidden tab does ring. This
pod's own messages ring nothing. The first answer of a session rings for
nothing, so Log in is silent whatever waits, and so does a room that is
new to the list. One answer rings once at most, however much is new in
it. What the shell has rung for is kept in RAM, for the pod of the
session, and is forgotten when the session closes. Only this poll rings:
the chat pages' own reads of the room list do not, and the other
notifications have no sound. Since 2026-11-24 (section 11; 4.17) the
poll's read of the chat rooms asks only for what is new, and what the
shell looks at for the sound is the chat list in memory, once that
read's answer was put into it. What rings is the same: something that
another read put into the list rings at the poll's next read, as it did
before. Since 2026-11-24, too (section 11; 4.19), a room has a new
newest message when the position of that message has risen
(`lastMessage.position`), where the shell looked at the room's highest
position (`lastPosition`): an edit or a delete of a message is a row of
its own and raises the highest position, and it rings nothing.

When the sound cannot ring. A browser lets a page make sound only after
the person has touched the page, so the sound engine is made at the
first click, end of a touch or key press in the tab, and nothing plays
before it; a person with an open session has tapped Log in. The sound
plays only while the wallet's page is running. A phone with another app
in front, or a locked phone, plays nothing: the phone's browser freezes
the page. On a computer a hidden tab plays it up to about a minute late
(Chrome's rule for a hidden tab's timers). On an iPhone, Safari stops a
page's sound when it leaves the screen; the wallet starts the engine
again when the page is back, and at the next tap if Safari refuses that,
so after coming back the sound may need one tap before it plays again.
Something new that comes while the engine is stopped is not rung for
later. Whether the iPhone's silent switch mutes the sound was not
checked. A sound or a banner while the wallet is not open would need
push notifications, which are not built (section 10).

The sound's switch is the fourth row of the Account page (8.2, Account),
"Sound: on" or "Sound: off". The sound is on until the person turns it
off, and the choice is kept on that phone or computer, in localStorage
under `anopod-wallet.sound`, for the device and not per pod. Turning it
on plays the sound once, so the person hears what it is. While it is off
the shell still keeps track of what is new, and rings nothing.

The next-step rule, applied after an unlock and after each step
finishes:

    not vouched                                   /vouching
    vouched, setup not complete                   /identity
    setup complete, bucketOneImages = 0           /account/recovery/selfie
    bucketTwoImages = 0 or bucketTwoInfos < 3     /account/recovery/details
    otherwise                                     /wallet

After an unlock, Wallet reads Home: the landing page sends a pod whose
next step is /wallet to /home, while the setup steps (the recovery
walkthrough's "Go to wallet") still end at Wallet, the next thing to do
(2026-11-06, section 11).

The user may navigate anywhere the navigation shows at any time.

The toolbar's words and the navigation's labels come from the
dictionary and follow the language (8.8; 2026-11-06, section 11).

The Update button (2026-11-22, section 11; the plan is
forclaude/wallet-refresh-plan-1.md). A page of the wallet keeps the code
it was loaded with for as long as it lives. In a browser tab a person
reloads it. A wallet opened from a phone's Home Screen (section 2) has
no address bar and no reload button, and the phone keeps its page for
days, so such a wallet ran an old build until the app was swiped away.
The wallet now finds a newer build by itself (update.service, 8.3): it
asks its own server for the page again, past the browser's own copy
(`fetch('/')` with `cache: 'no-store'`), and reads the name of the
script file in the answer. A build has one script file, named by its
content (`main-`, letters and digits, `.js`), so another name than the
one this page runs is another build. Nothing changes on the server for
it, and the page's content rules allow the ask (`connect-src 'self'`,
section 2). It asks once when the page starts, every 5 minutes while the
page is on the screen (`UPDATE_CHECK_MS`), and each time the page comes
back to the front (the browser's `visibilitychange`; a phone freezes a
page's timers while another app is in front). It never asks while the
page is hidden, and once a newer build was seen it asks no more. An
answer that names no script file changes nothing. A development build
has one script with no content name (`main.js`): the check is off
there, so `ng serve` asks nothing. While a newer build is there, the
top bar shows a filled button "Update" (`shell.update`, "อัปเดต"), after
the spacer and before the username, on every page, the first page too.
On a screen narrower than 600 px the username is not shown while the
button is there, and the wallet's name is cut with "…" when the row has
no room (Thai at 360 and 375 px; English fits from 360 up). Both rules
hold only while the button shows (the class `updating` on the toolbar).
Since 2026-11-24 (section 11) the wallet's name is the one short word
"anoPod" in letters of 18 px, which has room beside the button from 320
px up in both languages and in the staff's editions, so the second rule
finds nothing to cut on a phone.
The button has 12 px at each side where Material gives 24, so it is 70
px wide in English and 64 in Thai. A tap refreshes at once, with no
question in between (the refresh, the paragraph after the next). A
person who does not tap keeps the old code and the button.

The end of a login (2026-11-22, section 11; the same plan). The
masterpod keeps one pair of session keys for an anoPod, for some hours,
and a page whose keys it no longer took went on looking logged in, with
red lines such as "HTTP 401: session expired" on its pages. The shell
now tells the person. The end of a login is the masterpod's 401 on the
status read of the 5-second poll (/check-anopod-status; 8.2,
Notifications) with one of three reasons: `session expired` (the hours
are over, or a finished recovery ended the session), `bad signature`
(the keys the masterpod holds are those of a newer login of the same
anoPod, on another phone or computer) or `unknown anopod` (the anoPod
is gone). On that read `bad signature` can only mean the session keys.
Three things are not an end and are passed over as before: no
connection, a masterpod that is down, and a phone whose clock is wrong
(`timestamp outside window`). Before the box shows, the shell asks the
status once more, and only a second answer with one of the three
reasons counts: a read that was on its way while the same tab logged in
anew (Setup, the finish of a recovery) is then not taken for the end.
The poll also runs at once when the page comes back to the front, so
the box is there before a tap. The box is the wallet's pop-up box with
one button (`single`, 8.9). Its title is "You are logged out"
(`shell.loggedOutTitle`), its one sentence "A login ends by itself after
some hours. It also ends when your anoPod is logged in on another phone
or computer. Log in again to go on." (`shell.loggedOutText`), and its
button "OK" (`shell.ok`). In Thai: "คุณออกจากระบบแล้ว";
"การเข้าสู่ระบบจะสิ้นสุดเองเมื่อผ่านไปหลายชั่วโมง
และจะสิ้นสุดเมื่อ anoPod ของคุณเข้าสู่ระบบบนโทรศัพท์หรือคอมพิวเตอร์เครื่องอื่นด้วย
โปรดเข้าสู่ระบบอีกครั้งเพื่อดำเนินการต่อ"; "ตกลง". The sentence names no number of
hours: the number is the masterpod's setting, and the wallet does not
know it. Whatever closes the box, OK or a step back in the browser's
history, the wallet locks and refreshes (the next paragraph). The poll
waits while the box is open, so there is one box. The recovery page
(/recover/case, 12.3) has a session of its own and keeps its own
sentence; the box does not show there.

The refresh (2026-11-22, section 11; the same plan). Three things end in
it: a tap on the Update button, the box "You are logged out", and Lock.
Until 2026-11-22 Lock dropped the session's keys and showed the first
page inside the app, and no page was loaded; Log in loads none either. A
refresh is a real load of the page (`location.reload()`), which empties
the page's whole memory and brings the newest build, and it always ends
on the first page, with Log in and Create account. Meanwhile the words
"Refreshing…" (`shell.refreshing`, "กำลังรีเฟรช…") stand in the middle of
the screen, over the whole page (a `div` with the class `refreshing` in
the shell, with the role `status`). The page is loaded again only after
the wallet's server has answered: update.service asks the server for
the page first and waits 5 seconds at most (`REFRESH_WAIT_MS`). With no
answer the words go away and the wallet stays as it is, because a
wallet from the Home Screen has no reload button to get off a browser's
error page. Every refresh starts from the first page: the shell drops
the session and shows the first page inside the app (`toFirstPage()` in
app.ts), and then the page is loaded again; without that, a refresh
tapped on the Create page came back on the Create page. Lock does this
at once, as before, and then asks the server, so with no connection
Lock still locks and the wallet stays on the first page it shows. The
Update button asks the server first, so with no connection a tap
changes nothing and a session stays open. A browser's own reload button
does what it always did. One workaround stands beside the refresh, and
it is not a design. In Chrome's app window on Android (the wallet opened
from its Home screen icon) every load of the page inside that window
leaves the shell 56 px higher than the window (901.3 on a window of 845,
seen on an emulator), and one swipe then takes the top bar off the
screen: the after-production list's item "the wallet as an app on
Android: the top bar leaves after a pulled-down reload". A refresh is
such a load. So after a start the shell looks three times, after 0.3, 1
and 3 seconds, whether it is higher than the window, and if so writes
its height onto itself (`100dvh`, the same height its style sheet
names), which Chrome then works out anew. Where the shell fits the
window nothing is written.

### 8.2 The screens

Landing. One outlined card, at most 560 px wide, centred on the page,
its content centred, the same in every edition; nothing stands above it
(the test-site notice is gone; 2026-11-13, section 11). From the top of
the card: the logo, the picture public/logo.png in a box 72 px high
(alt text "anoPod"); the headline "Your anoPod" at 1.75 rem, weight
500; the subtitle "Log in with your passkey, or create a new anoPod" in
the muted colour; two buttons, stacked, each as wide as the card's content
and 48 px high, "Log in" (filled, a fingerprint icon before the word)
and "Create account" (outlined); then one small line, "Lost your
passkey?" and the text link "Recover account" in the primary colour.
While a log-in runs, a progress bar and "Logging in…" show above the
buttons; after a failure, the error in red and "No passkey for this
site on this device? Create an anoPod instead." Every word follows the
language; under the card, while the app is in Thai, the button "Switch
to English" (8.8). Log in: /challenge (unlock), the passkey assertion
with the PRF salt, /unlock; opens blob1, chatPrivateKeyBlob and
identityBlob; then /check-anopod-status and the next-step rule. Since
2026-11-18 (4.8; section 11) the /unlock payload carries addedPasskeys:
true, and any passkey of the anoPod logs in, the main one or an added
one. There are two ways to the key blob key (section 7). The main
passkey makes it from its PRF output, as before. For an added passkey
the masterpod answers wrappedKeyBlobKey, that passkey's own copy, and
the wallet opens it under a key from the passkey's PRF output; a copy
that does not open stops the log-in with "/unlock: this passkey's copy
of the key blob key does not open", and no key is made in its place.
blob1 opens under KEK_prf either way: the masterpod answers the blob1
of the passkey that signed. The credential id of that passkey is kept
for the tab (session.service, 8.3), and the Passkeys page marks it.
Since 2026-11-20 (4.11; section 11) a login of a vouched anoPod whose
setup is complete ends by storing the first key blob, pair one alone,
of each of its anos accounts that has none yet; the person sees nothing
of it, and a failure there is passed over, so the login goes through
either way. The
platform's passkey picker is what says whether a passkey exists; with
none, the authenticator's own message shows and the page suggests
Create. Create goes to /create, Recover to /recover.

Create, a linear Material stepper
1. "Step 1 of creating your anoPod is to become vouched. We do this to
   keep the anoSphere safe and secure." First name, last name. Next.
2. Username: checked as typed through /check-username, debounced 400
   ms, "available" or "taken" shown; Next enabled when available.
3. Selfie: the camera component (section 8.4), preview, retake. Next.
4. Create: one button: /challenge (create), the passkey registration
   with the PRF extension, the two ephemeral keys, /create-anopod. On
   201: the session is open; "Your anoPod is created, now get vouched",
   Continue to /vouching. If the registration returned a PRF output it is
   kept; otherwise setup will unlock first, as the test app does.

Vouching. Title "Get vouched". Until vouched: the subtitle "Someone who
already has an anoPod confirms they know you."; the status line
(vouchCount) refreshed by the notification poll (every 5 s, as today);
the instructions in three parts, "How vouching works" (every anoPod is
vouched for by a real person who already has one; two vouches from seeds
or one from a super seed, which also makes the pod a seed), "What to do"
(ask a couple of people in the anoSphere for their username, search each
one, check the photo and the tag, Send request) and "While you wait" (the
page changes by itself, Log in brings the pod back here until vouched, a
decline shows under Notifications); then a username search
(/search-usernames) showing the profile card with the selfie and the seed
flags, a Send request button (/send-vouch-request), and the requests sent
this session. Once vouched, all of that is gone and the card shows only a
big "You've been vouched", "N people vouched for you. You can continue to
the next step." (1 person when it is one) and a big Continue to
/identity. A seed approving or declining uses /seed.

Identity, three panes
1. Why: the plain-English explanation, in these points: step 6 of setup
   is your public ledger id; we do not store what you type; it is turned
   into a one-way hash on your device; the hash is kept encrypted by
   independent keyholders, not in our database; it exists so you, or one
   day your heirs, can prove this identity made this account after a
   complete lockout, and recover the account and its anos; it cannot be
   deleted, by anyone, ever, and you have to know that before you go on;
   a very sophisticated attack could leak a hash of your birth record,
   and there are far easier ways to learn a birthday or a maiden name.
   A checkbox "I understand this record can never be deleted" and
   Continue, enabled by the checkbox.
2. The form, docs/public-ledger-id.md section 1: the nine fields, a
   Known / Unknown select beside the five that allow it, a country
   select, a date picker. Above it: write things the common way they
   are written today, your best guess of your birth certificate; St.
   Louis or Saint Louis both can be tried in a recovery, but the more
   exact, the easier; if you do not know, choose Unknown. Submit.
3. Review: every answer as given. "Check that everything is right. If
   this is wrong, you may not be able to recover after a complete
   lockout, and your heirs may fail to recover it in the future." Edit
   goes back; "All information is correct" computes the PLID and the
   lookup id (scrypt takes well under a second), drops the answers, and
   goes to /setup.

Setup. A Start button. In order: generate the encryption key, the backup
code, the backup code keys, the chat pair, blob1, blob2,
chatPrivateKeyBlob, identityBlob (if the PRF output is not in RAM, an
unlock first). Five of the eight show as a progress list; the backup
code, its keys and blob2 have no line (2026-11-10, section 11). Then,
with no stop in between: deposit the backup code (section 6,
backupcode), then /complete-setup with the eight fields; on 200 drop the
code and go on by the next-step rule. The backup code is never shown:
until 2026-11-10 the page showed it once in groups of four with "I have
written it down, complete" and waited for that button. On an Android phone
(the browser's user agent string says Android; 2026-11-07, section 11)
the page does not leave yet: once /complete-setup has answered, the card
shows "Protect your passkey" in place of the progress list: "Strongly
recommended." in bold, then "It is free, it takes a few minutes, and it
makes your anoPod much harder to steal."; the why, "On an Android phone
your passkey is usually kept by Google, under your Google account. If
someone takes over that Google account, your passkey is within their
reach."; what it does, "Google's Advanced Protection makes that takeover
very hard: signing in to Google needs your passkey or a security key,
account recovery is slow and strict, and most outside apps are kept
out."; the caution, "It changes how you sign in to Google, and a few
apps that use your Google account may stop working. Google's page
explains it before you turn it on."; the button "Open Google's Advanced
Protection", which opens https://landing.google.com/advancedprotection/
in a new tab; "Then choose one:" over two radio choices, "I turned it
on" and "Skip for now"; and Continue, off until one is picked, which
goes on by the next-step rule. The answer is recorded in the wallet
settings on the masterpod (4.7; 2026-11-07, section 11), 'on' or
'skipped'; the wallet cannot check what the person did; the pane shows
once, at setup, and never on an iPhone or a computer. Google's Advanced
Protection for the Google account is meant, not Android 16's device
setting of the same name. A /complete-setup refused with 409 leaves at
once, as before, without the pane. A failed deposit shows Retry (section
6, step 3). A /complete-setup refused with 409 setup already complete
means a dropped answer earlier: /check-anopod-status, and if setup is
complete, carry on.

Account recovery, one linear Material stepper, at
/account/recovery/selfie (opened at step 1) and /account/recovery/details
(opened at step 2). Titled "Account recovery", with "Everything here is
encrypted on your phone before it is sent. Nobody at anoPod can read it."
above the steps. It replaced the two bucket pages on 2026-11-05 (section
11); the server calls are the same.
1. Selfie. "Take a selfie." and a "Why do we need this?" button that
   opens the longer text (what a moderator compares it with, the key only
   the keyholders can rebuild, up to five, one is enough). The camera
   component in high quality, front camera, up to five, preview and
   remove. Next runs bucket one's flow: a fresh bucket key and keyId;
   each image encrypted under the key; the deposits (securitybucket1);
   /add-to-security-bucket-one with keyId and the images; on 201 the key
   is dropped, the status re-read, and the stepper moves on. With a
   selfie already on file and none pending, Next just moves on.
2. ID. The reminder "The more you add here, the easier it will be to
   recover your account if you are ever locked out." Then "Now a photo of
   your ID. The best ones show your photo and your full name, like a
   driver's license, a national or state ID card, or a passport. Lay it
   flat on a table and fill the frame. Things that do not prove who you
   are, like a bus pass, do not help." The camera component in normal
   quality, back camera, preview and remove. No Back here, the selfie is
   sent.
3. Email. "An email address where you can be reached if you are locked
   out of your account."
4. Phone. "A phone number where you can be reached."
5. Friend or family. Their name and their phone number, both or neither;
   "A moderator may phone them to check that it is really you. Someone
   like a spouse, or someone who lives with you, is best."
6. Bank account, optional, with Skip. Bank, name on the account, account
   number, all three or skip. "A bank account in your name is strong
   proof. In a recovery a moderator can send two small deposits and ask
   you the amounts. The name on the account should match the name on
   your ID." and "This is encrypted on your phone. Nobody at anoPod can
   read it. It is only opened in a recovery you ask for."
7. Anything else, optional. The camera again, back camera (the ID photos
   and these share the five per visit), free lines one per line, and the
   reminder once more. Finish runs bucket two's flow with everything
   gathered: the photos, and one info entry per piece, "phone: ...",
   "email: ...", "contact: name, phone", "bank: bank, name, number", then
   each extra line; the deposits (securitybucket2);
   /add-to-security-bucket-two; on 201 the key is dropped and the status
   re-read.
Then the done view: "Done. On file for a recovery: 1 selfie, 2 photos
and 4 details." (the status counts), "You can add more any time under
Account." and Go to wallet, by the next-step rule.

On a first visit, until the details are on file (an image and three
infos, the next-step rule's line), steps 2 to 5 are required: each Next
waits for its piece, and Finish for all four. After that every step is
optional, Finish needs at least one new thing, and with nothing new it
reads Done and shows the done view without a call. Nothing leaves the
phone before Next on the selfie and Finish at the end, so Back costs
nothing; each send makes one key with the keyholders, which is why the
details go in one batch. A failed deposit or call shows the error and
Retry, which starts that send again with a fresh key.

Account. "Your account", at /account, in the navigation once setup is
complete, after DAO. Since 2026-11-18 (section 11; the plan is
forclaude/wallet-account-page-plan-1.md) the page is a plain list under
its title, with no subtitle and no sentence: one row per thing, each
with an icon, a title and one line, and a new row goes under the last
one. Five rows. "Account recovery", with the icon lock_reset (the one
the Cases page gives a recovery case) and the line "Your recovery
selfie and details", opens the Account recovery page, /account/recovery
(below). "Passkeys" (2026-11-18, section 11), with a key icon and the
line "See your passkeys, or add a spare", opens the Passkeys page,
/account/passkeys (below). "Public ledger id" (2026-11-18, section 11),
with the icon fingerprint (the one the case pages give a shared lookup
id) and the line "Check the birth record you gave at setup", opens the
Public ledger id page, /account/ledger-id (below). "Sound: on"
(2026-11-19, section 11), with the icon volume_up and the line "A short
sound when a chat message or a chat request arrives while the wallet is
open. Tap to turn it on or off on this phone or computer.", is the
switch of the wallet's sound (8.1). It is a button where the other four
are links, and it opens no page. A style rule of the page takes the
browser's own button look off it, the outline and the centred words, so
it is drawn as the link rows are: Material does that only inside
an action list, and this row stands in the nav list. A tap turns the
sound off: the title
then reads "Sound: off" and the icon is volume_off. The next tap turns
it on again and plays the sound once. The choice is kept on the device
(sound.service, 8.3). "Security alerts" (2026-11-21, section 11), with
the icon notifications_active and the line "An email and a notification
on your phone when a transfer starts to wait", opens the Security alerts
page, /account/alerts (below). No row has a
condition of its own: Account is in the navigation only once setup is
complete. A pod that reaches the Passkeys page earlier by its address
sees the masterpod's refusal there, and one that reaches the Public
ledger id page earlier sees that page's one red sentence. The page
reads nothing: what is on file shows on the Account recovery page.
Until 2026-11-18 the page carried the subtitle "Account recovery", the
sentence that now stands on the Account recovery page, and the two
recovery rows themselves.

The Account recovery page (2026-11-18, section 11), at
/account/recovery, reached from the Account page's first row. Titled
"Account recovery", Back to Account (the navigation's word,
"Account"), then "These are what a moderator would use to give your
account back if you were ever locked out. The more you add, the easier
it will be to recover your account." and two rows, Recovery selfie and
Recovery details, opening the walkthrough above at step 1 or step 2,
each with what the status counts on file ("1 selfie on file", "2
photos and 4 details on file", "None on file yet"). The status only
counts, since everything is encrypted, so the rows say how many, never
which. The next-step rule (8.1) and Home's Things to do do not pass
this page: they open the walkthrough directly.

Protect your passkey (2026-11-07, section 11), at /account/protect,
reached from Home's Things to do on an Android phone while the recorded
answer is skipped: the setup pane again, titled "Protect your passkey",
Back to Home, then the pane's lines from `common` ("Strongly
recommended." in bold with the benefits, the why, what it does, the
caution, the button "Open Google's Advanced Protection" to Google's page
in a new tab, "Then choose one:" over "I turned it on" and "Skip for
now") and Save, off until one is picked, which records the answer in the
wallet settings (4.7, settings.service) as 'on' or 'skipped' and goes to
Home; a refusal in red. No row under Account.

Passkeys (2026-11-18, section 11; the plan is
forclaude/add-passkey-plan-1.md, and the masterpod's side is 4.8), at
/account/passkeys, reached from the Account page's Passkeys row and from
the notification "A passkey was added to your anoPod". Titled
"Passkeys", Back to Account (the navigation's word, "Account"), then "A
passkey is what unlocks your anoPod. You can add another one: a spare
security key, or a passkey kept with Apple when your first one is kept
with Google. Every passkey here unlocks this same anoPod."

The list is read on open with /list-passkeys. A refusal shows in red
where the list would be, as "/list-passkeys: <reason>", and the three
buttons of the add stay off until the list is read. First the main
passkey, the one on the anoPod's row: a key icon, the fixed name "Main
passkey" and the line "The passkey this anoPod was made with, or the one
from its last recovery". It has no name of its own, no date and no
Rename. Then each added passkey, oldest first: a key icon, its name, the
line "Added Nov 18, 2026, 3:50:12 PM" (the moment of the add, in the
language's date form) and, beside the row, a pencil button whose label
is "Rename". The names are the wallet's own: they live in the wallet
settings (4.7, settings.service) as passkeyNames, a map by passkey id
(section 7), so the masterpod stores none and cannot read one; the
settings are read on open when they were not read yet. An added passkey
with no name there shows as "Passkey". The row of the passkey that
opened this session, the one whose credential id is the session's (8.3),
also shows the line "In use now". Rename draws that row as a small form
in the row's place: a text box labelled "Name" that holds the name
(empty for "Passkey"), Save and Cancel. The two buttons are one group
(2026-11-18, section 11): on a phone both stand under the box, and on a
wide screen both beside it. Save checks the name rule and
writes the settings with the new name beside the other names; a name
that breaks the rule shows "A name is 1 to 40 characters." in red under
the box, and a save that failed shows its reason there
("/set-wallet-settings: <reason>"). The name rule, for Rename and for
the add: the name trimmed, 1 to 40 characters, counted as whole
characters (Array.from), so a Thai letter or an emoji counts once.

The add, under the heading "Add a passkey": "Three taps: one with a
passkey you already have, then two with the new one. Have both at
hand." and "Keep the new passkey in a different place from the ones you
